title: Sealed-bid auctions
objectives: Compare first-price and second-price auctions and bid well in each.

screens.title: How much to bid
screens.prose: A sealed-bid auction: the higher bid wins and pays its own bid. You value the lot at £80. One rival has a value uniform from £0 to £100 and bids half of it. Drag your bid along the curve.

derive.caption: Bid £{{fixed(p1.x, 0)}}: you win with chance {{fixed(min(2 * p1.x / 100, 1), 2)}} and expect £{{fixed((80 - p1.x) * min(2 * p1.x / 100, 1), 2)}}.

screens.question: Which bid earns the most on average, in £?

hints.text: A higher bid wins more often but leaves less profit when it wins.
Your profit if you win is $80 - b$; you win when the rival's bid $V/2$ is below $b$.
The curve peaks at £40, where you expect £32.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Drag the point to the top of the curve.

byKey.value: Bidding £80 wins most often, but every win then pays £80 for an £80 lot: no profit.
byKey.fifty: At £50 you always win, but you earn only £30. Bidding £40 wins 80% of the time and earns £32.

explain.text: Your bid wins when the rival's bid, half a uniform value, is below it: chance $2b/100$. Expected profit $(80 - b) \cdot 2b/100$ peaks at $b = 40$, at £32. You shade your bid to half your value.

screens.title: Why half
screens.prose: Check the curve's peak by algebra, as `limits` l14-best-value does: set the slope to 0, then check the ends.
screens.question: Put the steps in order. Leave out the line that does not belong.

lines.text: You win when the rival's bid $V/2$ is below $b$: $P(\text{win}) = \dfrac{2b}{100}$ for $b \le 50$.
Expected profit is $(80 - b) \cdot \dfrac{2b}{100}$, since a win pays $80 - b$.
Its slope is $\dfrac{160 - 4b}{100}$, which is 0 at $b = 40$.
Check the ends: $b = 0$ earns 0 and $b = 50$ earns 30, both below 32.
Bid as much as possible, to make the chance of winning largest.
lines.why: Winning more often costs profit on every win. At £50 you always win but earn only £30.

hints.text: Start from the chance of winning.
Profit is the chance of winning times what a win pays.
Chance, profit, slope, ends.

feedback.correct: Chance, profit, slope 0 at £40, then the ends.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Begin with the chance that your bid wins.

byKey.d1: Winning more often costs profit on every win. At £50 you always win but earn only £30.
byKey.left-out: Every line but the one about winning as often as possible belongs.

explain.text: The chance of winning grows with $b$, and the profit per win shrinks. Their product has slope $(160 - 4b)/100$, zero at £40. Both ends earn less, so £40, half your value, is best.

screens.title: Pay the second price
screens.prose: Now the rules change. The highest bid wins but pays the **second-highest** bid. Your value is still £80. Try three bids against a rival's top bid of £70, then £90.
screens.question: Fill in your profit in £ for each bid. A loss is negative.

hints.text: You pay the rival's bid, not your own, when you win.
Against £70, any bid above 70 wins and pays 70: profit 10.

feedback.correct: Bidding £80 is never worse than shading or overbidding.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. When you win, you pay the rival's bid.

byKey.r0c2: £60 is below the rival's £70, so you lose a lot you would have bought at £70: profit 0.
byKey.r1c3: £95 beats £90, so you win and pay £90 for an £80 lot: −10.

explain.text: Shading to £60 loses a £10 profit when the rival bids £70. Overbidding to £95 buys a £10 loss when the rival bids £90. Your bid decides only whether you win, never what you pay, so bid your value.

screens.title: What the seller gets
screens.prose: Two bidders, values uniform from £0 to £100. Lesson `puzzles` l11 found the larger of two such values averages $\tfrac23 \times 100$ and the smaller $\tfrac13 \times 100$.
screens.question: Fill in the seller's expected price in each format, and your expected profit.

rows: First price: the winner bids half her value. Expected price?
Second price: the winner pays the other value. Expected price?
Second price, your value £80, one rival: your expected profit

hints.text: First price pays half the larger value; second price pays the smaller value.
Half of 66.67 is 33.33, and the smaller value averages 33.33.

feedback.correct: £33.33 both ways, and £32 for you: the same as first price.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the average of the larger and the smaller value.

byKey.r2c1: You win when the rival's value is below 80, chance 0.8. You then pay it, £40 on average: $0.8 \times 40 = 32$.

explain.text: First price pays half the larger value, $\tfrac12 \times 66.67 = 33.33$; second price pays the smaller, also 33.33. Your profit is £32 in both formats. This is **revenue equivalence**: with $n$ bidders the price averages $\tfrac{n - 1}{n + 1} \times 100$.

screens.title: Shade or not
screens.prose: A second-price auction. You value the lot at £80.
screens.question: What do you bid?

options.why: You shaded to make a profit. The profit already comes from paying the second price; shading only loses lots you wanted.
Overbidding wins only when the second bid is above £80, and then you pay more than the lot is worth.
Halving is the first-price rule against one rival. Here the rival's bid sets your price, so shading only loses lots.

hints.text: Ask what your bid changes: the price, or only whether you win.
In second price, you pay the other bid.
So bid exactly your value.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Your bid sets only whether you win.

byKey.b: You shaded to make a profit. The profit already comes from paying the second price; shading only loses lots you wanted.

explain.text: In a second-price auction your bid sets whether you win, never the price. Bidding £80 wins exactly the lots you want at a price below £80. The reverse slip, bidding £80 in a first-price auction, makes every win earn nothing.

screens.title: A reserve price
screens.prose: A second-price auction with a reserve of £50. No bid below £50 can win. The winner pays the larger of £50 and the second bid.
screens.question: Which is right?

options.text: The £40 bidder should not win, and the £70 bidder still bids £70
The £70 bidder should bid the reserve, £50
options.why: Bidding £50 loses whenever a rival bids between 50 and 70, lots worth a profit to you.

options.text: The £40 bidder should bid £50 to take part
options.why: Any win then costs at least £50 for a £40 lot: a loss of at least £10.

hints.text: A win always costs at least the reserve.
For the £40 bidder every win loses money.
Bidding your value still wins exactly the profitable lots.

feedback.correct: Right: bid your value, and a value below the reserve does not bid.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what each bidder pays when they win.

byKey.b: Bidding £50 loses whenever a rival bids between 50 and 70, lots worth a profit to you.

explain.text: A reserve is one more bid, the seller's, that you must beat. A bidder worth £40 loses on any win, so stays out. A bidder worth £70 still bids £70, for the same reason as before.

screens.title: Two formats, one price
screens.prose:
With $n$ bidders whose values are uniform from £0 to £100:

$$\text{second price: bid } v, \qquad \text{first price: bid } \tfrac{n - 1}{n}\,v, \qquad E[\text{price}] = \tfrac{n - 1}{n + 1} \times 100$$

The first-price bid is what the second-highest value is worth, on average, given yours is the highest.
screens.question: Three bidders, first price, value £90. What do you bid?

options.why: You halved your value, the two-bidder rule. With three bidders you shade by a third.
Bidding your value is the second-price rule. Here a win would earn nothing.
Three quarters is the four-bidder rule. With three bidders bid two thirds.

hints.text: Use $\tfrac{n - 1}{n}\,v$.
$n = 3$, so two thirds.
$\tfrac23 \times 90 = 60$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply your value by $(n - 1)/n$.

explain.text: With three bidders shade to $\tfrac23$ of your value: £60. More bidders mean less shading. Either way the seller expects $\tfrac{n - 1}{n + 1} \times 100$.

screens.title: Drill
screens.prose: Four auctions, about three minutes each, as an interview allows. Say the reasoning aloud before you answer. Values are uniform from £0 to £100.

state.caption: The values in the last question.

screens.question: Fill in the four answers, in £.

rows: Three bidders, first price, value £60: your bid
Five bidders, first price, value £90: your bid
Four bidders, either format: the expected price
Second price, values £30, £55 and £72, each bid truthfully: the price paid

hints.text: Bid $\tfrac{n - 1}{n}\,v$ in first price; the price averages $\tfrac{n - 1}{n + 1} \times 100$.
$\tfrac23 \times 60$, $\tfrac45 \times 90$, $\tfrac35 \times 100$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first answer that is marked.

byKey.r1c1: With five bidders shade by a fifth: $\tfrac45 \times 90 = 72$.
byKey.r3c1: The £72 bidder wins and pays the second bid, £55, not her own.

explain.text: First price: $\tfrac23 \times 60 = 40$ and $\tfrac45 \times 90 = 72$. With four bidders the price averages $\tfrac35 \times 100 = 60$. In the second-price auction the £72 bidder wins and pays £55.

screens.title: Follow-up: more bidders
screens.prose: The interviewer adds bidders: ten of them now, values uniform from £0 to £100, first price. With ten bidders you bid $\tfrac{9}{10}$ of your value.
screens.question: What price does the seller expect, in £?

hints.text: Use $\tfrac{n - 1}{n + 1} \times 100$ with $n = 10$.
$\tfrac{9}{11} \times 100$.

byKey.bid: £90 uses 0.9, the share of your value you bid. The price is that share of the top value, which averages $\tfrac{10}{11} \times 100$.

explain.text: The top of ten values averages $\tfrac{10}{11} \times 100$, and the winner bids nine tenths of it: $\tfrac{9}{11} \times 100 = 81.82$. A dealer's sealed bid for a client's portfolio is a first-price auction. An English auction ends near the second-highest value.

ideas: In a second-price auction bid your value: your bid decides only whether you win.
In a first-price auction with $n$ uniform bidders, shade to $\tfrac{n - 1}{n}$ of your value.
Both formats give the seller the same expected price, $\tfrac{n - 1}{n + 1} \times 100$.
summary.trap: Shading in a second-price auction. The price comes from the other bid, so shading only loses lots you wanted.

quiz.prose: A second-price auction with four bidders whose values are £20, £45, £61 and £38. Everyone bids their value.
quiz.question: What does the winner pay, in £?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The winner pays the next bid down.

byKey.own: £61 is the winner's own bid. In second price she pays the next bid, £45.

explain.text: The £61 bidder wins and pays the second-highest bid, £45.

quiz.prose: A first-price auction with six bidders, values uniform from £0 to £100. Your value is £72.
quiz.question: What do you bid, in £?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Bid $\tfrac{n - 1}{n}$ of your value.

byKey.half: Halving is the two-bidder rule. With six bidders shade by a sixth.
byKey.value: Bidding your value in first price makes every win earn nothing.

explain.text: With six bidders shade to $\tfrac56$ of your value: $\tfrac56 \times 72 = 60$.

quiz.prose: Seven bidders with values uniform from £0 to £100.
quiz.question: What price does the seller expect, in £, in either format?

byKey.top: 87.5 is the average top value, $\tfrac78 \times 100$. The price is the second value, or the shaded top bid.

explain.text: With $n = 7$ the price averages $\tfrac{6}{8} \times 100 = 75$. Second price pays the second value, which averages 75. First price pays $\tfrac67$ of the top, $\tfrac67 \times 87.5 = 75$.
